summary:
Harpyja is a farm management prototype that helps farmers register their properties, map their fields, and manage planting and harvest records. It connects these records with NASA Earth observation data through an interactive dashboard, allowing users to explore historical conditions and compare observations across dates and fields.

The system integrates NASA POWER, GPM/IMERG, SMAP, ECOSTRESS, and HLS data to present weather, rainfall, soil moisture, and vegetation information. It shows data availability and spatial resolution so users can understand the limitations of each source.

Harpyja addresses the practical challenge of making space-based agricultural information easier to access alongside everyday farm records. Its purpose is to help farmers understand their fields and ask better-informed questions when planning and reviewing crop cycles. The prototype uses demonstration farm records and real NASA data; benefits for farmers have not yet been measured.

I intend to continue developing Harpyja personally, test it with farmers, and make it available free of charge to smallholder farmers.
details:
Harpyja is a farm management prototype designed to bring everyday agricultural records and NASA Earth observation data into one application. I developed it around a simple goal: help farmers register their properties, manage planting and harvest activities, and explore the environmental conditions associated with their fields.

How it works

Users register a farm, define its fields by drawing boundaries on a map, and associate crops and growing seasons with each area. They can record planting dates, planted areas, harvest progress, and production, creating a history of each crop cycle.

An interactive dashboard connects field locations with NASA data sources:

- NASA POWER: historical weather and solar radiation information.

- GPM/IMERG: precipitation estimates.

- SMAP: surface and root-zone soil moisture information, depending on the product.

- ECOSTRESS: land surface temperature and evapotranspiration-related information.

- HLS: surface reflectance used to calculate vegetation indices such as NDVI and EVI.

Users can select historical periods, explore maps and time series, and compare vegetation observations across fields on common valid dates. The application stores retrieved data in PostgreSQL so previously collected history remains available for subsequent analysis.

The prototype also includes crop planning and an AI-assisted field advisory feature. These use farm records and available environmental evidence to organize explanations and suggested follow-up actions. They do not provide validated yield forecasts or replace professional agronomic assessment.

Benefits and intended impact

Harpyja aims to reduce the effort required to consult farm records and environmental data separately. Bringing them together can help farmers review crop cycles, identify changes that deserve field inspection, and prepare better-informed questions for technical advisers.

Smallholder farmers are the intended long-term audience. I plan to continue developing the project personally, test it with farmers, and make the system available free of charge. These are future objectives: adoption, usability benefits, and improvements in agricultural outcomes have not yet been measured.

Technology and development

The project uses TypeScript, React and Next.js for the web interface; Java and Quarkus for the backend; PostgreSQL and PostGIS for persistent records and spatial calculations; and React Native with Expo for the mobile application. Leaflet supports interactive maps. NASA services supply environmental data, while Mistral supports the advisory functionality. The mobile version still requires validation on physical devices.

The original concept, motivation, and objectives are mine. AI tools assisted development and the preparation of documentation and presentation materials.

Creative approach and design considerations

Harpyja’s creative approach is to use the farmer’s own field boundaries and crop history as the context for exploring space-based information. The same field connects property management, planting, harvest, and environmental history.

Scientific limitations guided the design. Satellite products retain their native spatial resolution, and clipping a dataset to a field does not create finer detail. Missing observations remain missing rather than becoming zero, and incomplete periods are identified. Historical data are distinguished from forecasts.

The prototype also distinguishes fictitious demonstration farm records from real NASA data. Other considerations included traceable data sources, protection of credentials, separation of farm records, and connectivity limitations. These choices support transparent interpretation while leaving room for further testing and development.
